name: Selective Perception
description: What people think they are seeing is filtered by loyalties, expectations, and prior beliefs. Two people can witness the same event yet experience meaningfully different versions of it.
design_relevance_note: Important in user research, stakeholder synthesis, concept reviews, moderation, and interpretation of qualitative evidence: what participants or teams notice in the same screen, prototype, or incident can diverge because perception is already theory-laden.
myth_risk_note: Gerber & Green (1999) directly argue that more recent research calls the selective-perception hypothesis into question and finds limited support for its extreme formulations, suggesting some effects attributed to the label may instead reflect rational Bayesian updating on ambiguous information rather than a distinct perceptual bias.
prevalence_note: The phrase is broadly recognizable inside research, media, and organizational discussions about interpretation bias, even if designers more often encounter its sub-mechanisms under other names.

findings.description: Princeton and Dartmouth students watching the same rough football game reported sharply different numbers and sources of infractions, indicating that prior loyalties and commitments shape what people perceive in the very same event.
findings.source_title: They saw a game; a case study.
findings.source_venue: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
